items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Lorenz curve"?
options: A curve showing the cumulative percentage of income (or wealth) received by cumulative percentages of the population, ranked from poorest to richest
Payments from the government to individuals, such as pensions and unemployment benefits, with no good or service provided in return
The unequal distribution of the stock of assets, such as property, shares and savings, net of debts
The percentage of tax paid on an additional unit of income
items.answer: A curve showing the cumulative percentage of income (or wealth) received by cumulative percentages of the population, ranked from poorest to richest
items.markingKey: A. "Lorenz curve" is a curve showing the cumulative percentage of income (or wealth) received by cumulative percentages of the population, ranked from poorest to richest.

items.stem: Explain why wealth inequality is generally greater than income inequality.
items.answer: Wealth is a stock built up over time; high earners save more, returns on assets compound and assets are inherited, whereas many households have little or negative net wealth.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Wealth is a stock built up over time; high earners save more, returns on assets compound and assets are inherited, whereas many households have little or negative net wealth. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between income and wealth.
items.answer: Income is a flow of earnings over a period (wages, rent, interest, profit); wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time, net of debts.
items.markingKey: Income is a flow of earnings over a period (wages, rent, interest, profit); wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time, net of debts. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which inequality in Brazil shows measurement of income inequality.
items.answer: Brazil's Gini coefficient fell from about 0.59 in 2001 to about 0.52 by 2015, partly due to Bolsa Família and minimum wage rises, and remains among the highest in the world. A falling Gini shows the Lorenz curve moving closer to the line of equality as low incomes grew faster
items.markingKey: Context (Brazil's Gini coefficient fell from about 0.59 in 2001 to about 0.52 by 2015, partly due to Bolsa Família and minimum wage rises, and remains among the highest in the world.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A falling Gini shows the Lorenz curve moving closer to the line of equality as low incomes grew faster – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to measurement of income inequality.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate a Lorenz curve and how the Gini coefficient is derived from it, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Cumulative % of population (x) against cumulative % of income (y); 45° line of perfect equality; Lorenz curve below it; Gini = A/(A + B), where A is the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve; a curve further from the diagonal means more inequality.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Cumulative % of population (x) against cumulative % of income (y); 45° line of perfect equality; Lorenz curve below it; Gini = A/(A + B), where A is the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve; a curve further from the diagonal means more inequality. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the Gini coefficient is the best measure of inequality.
items.answer: It is the most widely used single measure, but it should be supplemented with quintile ratios, the Palma ratio and wealth data.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: single, comparable summary of the whole distribution; widely published; easy to track over time. Arguments against: insensitive to where inequality occurs; crossing Lorenz curves can give equal Ginis; depends on income vs consumption data; ignores wealth and non-income dimensions. Supported judgement: It is the most widely used single measure, but it should be supplemented with quintile ratios, the Palma ratio and wealth data.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "income inequality".
items.answer: The unequal distribution of income (a flow) among households or individuals in an economy
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the unequal distribution of income (a flow) among households or individuals in an economy. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: In Sundara, income is distributed as follows: Q1 4%, Q2 9%, Q3 20%, Q4 21%, Q5 46% (Q1 = poorest 20% of households). State the cumulative share of income received by the poorest 60% of households, and calculate the ratio of the income share of the richest 20% to that of the poorest 20%.
items.answer: Poorest 60% receive 33%; S80/S20 ratio = 46/4 = 11.5
items.markingKey: 4 + 9 + 20 = 33%; 46/4 = 11.5. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for both values. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant.

items.stem: What is a measure of relative poverty?
items.answer: The percentage of households with income below 60% of the median
items.markingKey: The percentage of households with income below 60% of the median. Relative poverty is relative to national incomes.

items.stem: Distinguish between relative poverty and absolute poverty.
items.answer: Absolute poverty is income below the level needed for basic needs, the same real threshold everywhere; relative poverty is income below a percentage of the national median, so it rises with the country's income level.
items.markingKey: Absolute poverty is income below the level needed for basic needs, the same real threshold everywhere; relative poverty is income below a percentage of the national median, so it rises with the country's income level. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that a country with no one below $3.00 a day has no poverty. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: People may still be in relative poverty, or multidimensionally poor, lacking health, education or decent housing.
items.markingKey: People may still be in relative poverty, or multidimensionally poor, lacking health, education or decent housing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: People may still be in relative poverty, or multidimensionally poor, lacking health, education or decent housing.

items.stem: Kalimar uses a relative poverty line of 50% of median income; median disposable income is $36,000. Ten households in a survey have incomes of $12,500, $13,500, $21,500, $27,600, $29,300, $42,000, $42,800, $44,500, $54,500, $60,000. Calculate the poverty line and the percentage of these households in relative poverty.
items.answer: Poverty line = 50% × $36,000 = $18,000; 2 of 10 households (20%) are below it.
items.markingKey: Line = 0.5 × 36,000 = 18,000; households below: $12,500, $13,500. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for 20%. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that relative poverty is a more useful measure than absolute poverty.
items.answer: Both are needed: absolute measures for global extreme poverty, relative measures for inclusion in high-income economies, supplemented by the MPI.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reflects social exclusion within a society; relevant in high-income countries; captures distribution. Arguments against: can rise as the economy grows; does not show material deprivation; absolute measures are essential for global comparisons (SDG 1). Supported judgement: Both are needed: absolute measures for global extreme poverty, relative measures for inclusion in high-income economies, supplemented by the MPI.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A UNDP/OPHI index measuring acute poverty through deprivations in health, education and living standards (10 indicators); a person is poor if deprived in at least one-third of weighted indicators"?
items.answer: Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI).

items.stem: Outline one way in which child poverty in the UK shows relative poverty in high-income countries.
items.answer: Around 4 million UK children (about 30%) lived in relative poverty after housing costs in 2022-23. Despite high average incomes, many households fall below 60% of median income, particularly after paying high rents
items.markingKey: Context (Around 4 million UK children (about 30%) lived in relative poverty after housing costs in 2022-23.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Despite high average incomes, many households fall below 60% of median income, particularly after paying high rents – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to relative poverty in high-income countries.

items.stem: According to the "Great Gatsby curve", countries with higher inequality tend to have:
items.answer: lower intergenerational income mobility
items.markingKey: lower intergenerational income mobility. Inequality of outcome reinforces inequality of opportunity.

items.stem: "Inequality is caused only by differences in effort." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Circumstances beyond individual control—family wealth, location, gender, discrimination and health—strongly shape incomes.
items.markingKey: Circumstances beyond individual control—family wealth, location, gender, discrimination and health—strongly shape incomes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Inequality is always harmful to an economy." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Some inequality provides incentives to work, train and innovate; the problem is excessive inequality and inequality of opportunity.
items.markingKey: Some inequality provides incentives to work, train and innovate; the problem is excessive inequality and inequality of opportunity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the gender pay gap and explain what it reveals about causes of income inequality.
items.answer: The OECD average gender gap in median earnings for full-time employees is around 11-12%. Occupational segregation, motherhood penalties and discrimination reduce women's earnings

items.stem: Outline one way in which caste and income in India shows discrimination as a cause of inequality and poverty.
items.answer: Studies find that Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe households in India have significantly lower average incomes and wealth than other groups. Social exclusion limits access to education, land and well-paid jobs

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that high levels of income inequality are an inevitable result of economic growth.
items.answer: Inequality is not inevitable; its level reflects institutions and policies as much as growth itself.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Kuznets curve: inequality rises in early industrialisation; returns to skills rise with technology; globalisation rewards capital. Arguments against: Nordic countries combine growth with low inequality; policy choices (taxes, transfers, education) matter; East Asian tigers grew with relatively low inequality. Supported judgement: Inequality is not inevitable; its level reflects institutions and policies as much as growth itself.

items.stem: Explain why high inequality may reduce economic growth.
items.answer: Poor households under-invest in education and health, wasting human capital; high inequality can reduce AD (the rich have lower MPC), and political instability may deter investment.

items.stem: Using the Great Gatsby curve (Miles Corak) as an example, explain consequences of inequality.
items.answer: Miles Corak and Alan Krueger showed that countries with high inequality, such as the USA and the UK, have lower intergenerational earnings mobility than Denmark or Finland. Unequal outcomes in one generation reduce opportunities for the next, perpetuating inequality

items.stem: What is a possible disadvantage of a high minimum wage?
items.answer: It may increase unemployment among low-skilled workers
items.markingKey: It may increase unemployment among low-skilled workers. Excess supply of labour at the higher wage.

items.stem: Distinguish between regressive taxation and progressive taxation.
items.answer: Under progressive taxation the average tax rate rises with income; under regressive taxation it falls, taking a larger share from low-income earners.
items.markingKey: Under progressive taxation the average tax rate rises with income; under regressive taxation it falls, taking a larger share from low-income earners. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between universal basic income and means-tested benefits.
items.answer: A UBI is paid to everyone unconditionally; means-tested benefits are targeted at households whose income or wealth is below a threshold and are withdrawn as income rises.
items.markingKey: A UBI is paid to everyone unconditionally; means-tested benefits are targeted at households whose income or wealth is below a threshold and are withdrawn as income rises. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the UK National Living Wage shows minimum wages as a policy against poverty.
items.answer: The UK raised its National Living Wage to £12.21 an hour for workers aged 21 and over from April 2025, targeting two-thirds of median earnings. Large rises raised low pay with limited evidence of job losses, though some firms cut hours or raised prices
items.markingKey: Context (The UK raised its National Living Wage to £12.21 an hour for workers aged 21 and over from April 2025, targeting two-thirds of median earnings.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Large rises raised low pay with limited evidence of job losses, though some firms cut hours or raised prices – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to minimum wages as a policy against poverty.

items.stem: "A minimum wage always increases unemployment." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: If set moderately, or where employers have monopsony power, minimum wages can raise pay with little or no loss of jobs, as many UK and US studies have found.
items.markingKey: If set moderately, or where employers have monopsony power, minimum wages can raise pay with little or no loss of jobs, as many UK and US studies have found. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Finland's basic income experiment shows universal basic income.
items.answer: In 2017-2018 Finland paid 2,000 unemployed people €560 a month unconditionally; employment effects were small but recipients reported better well-being and less stress. The trial suggested UBI improves well-being but is not a strong tool for raising employment
items.markingKey: Context (In 2017-2018 Finland paid 2,000 unemployed people €560 a month unconditionally; employment effects were small but recipients reported better well-being and less stress.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that progressive taxation is the best way to reduce income inequality.
items.answer: Progressive taxation is effective at reducing post-tax inequality, but long-run reductions require investment in human capital and fair labour markets.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: directly reduces the gap in post-tax incomes; raises revenue for transfers and services; automatic stabiliser. Arguments against: disincentives to work and invest; tax avoidance and capital flight; does not address inequality of opportunity; education and health spending tackle root causes. Supported judgement: Progressive taxation is effective at reducing post-tax inequality, but long-run reductions require investment in human capital and fair labour markets.

items.stem: You are an analyst at a regional development bank. A minister argues that a universal basic income is the most effective policy for reducing poverty. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: A UBI could complement but probably not replace targeted transfers, public services and education policies.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: simple, low administrative cost; no stigma or benefit traps; security in an age of automation. Counter-points: very expensive or too small to lift people out of poverty; untargeted: much goes to the non-poor; may require large tax rises; limited evidence on employment. Recommendation: A UBI could complement but probably not replace targeted transfers, public services and education policies. items.stem: Explain why universal basic income could reduce the disincentive effects of means-tested benefits.
items.answer: Means-tested benefits are withdrawn as income rises, creating high effective marginal tax rates; a UBI is not withdrawn, so recipients keep more of each extra dollar earned.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Means-tested benefits are withdrawn as income rises, creating high effective marginal tax rates; a UBI is not withdrawn, so recipients keep more of each extra dollar earned. items.stem: Under a proportional tax, the marginal tax rate is:
items.answer: equal to the average tax rate
items.markingKey: equal to the average tax rate. A constant rate on all income.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the marginal tax rate and the average tax rate.
items.answer: The marginal rate is the tax on the last (additional) dollar of income; the average rate is total tax as a percentage of total income.
items.markingKey: The marginal rate is the tax on the last (additional) dollar of income; the average rate is total tax as a percentage of total income. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that if I move into the 40% tax band, I will pay 40% tax on all my income. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Only the income above the threshold is taxed at 40%; income in lower bands is still taxed at the lower rates.
items.markingKey: Only the income above the threshold is taxed at 40%; income in lower bands is still taxed at the lower rates. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Oskaria has the following income tax bands on annual taxable income: $0–$8,000: 0%; $8,000–$30,000: 10%; $30,000–$80,000: 25%; above $80,000: 35%. Sana earns $36,000 a year. Calculate the tax paid and the average tax rate, and state whether the system is progressive.
items.answer: Tax = $3,700; average rate = 10.3%; progressive, because the average (and marginal) rate rises with income.
items.markingKey: Tax by bands = 3,700; ATR = 3,700/36,000 × 100 = 10.3%. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for 10.3%. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant. [R1] progressive.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that very high top marginal tax rates are an effective way to reduce inequality.
items.answer: Moderately higher top rates can reduce inequality, but very high rates may raise little revenue; closing loopholes and taxing wealth may be more effective.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: raise revenue from those most able to pay; reduce post-tax inequality; discourage excessive executive pay. Arguments against: tax avoidance and migration of high earners; disincentives to work and enterprise; revenue may fall if rates exceed the revenue-maximising level (Laffer curve). Supported judgement: Moderately higher top rates can reduce inequality, but very high rates may raise little revenue; closing loopholes and taxing wealth may be more effective.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a person moving into a higher tax band does not lose income overall.
items.answer: The higher marginal rate applies only to income above the band threshold, not to all income, so after-tax income still rises with each extra dollar (unless benefits are withdrawn).

items.stem: Briefly describe child poverty in the UK and explain what it reveals about relative poverty in high-income countries.
items.answer: Around 4 million UK children (about 30%) lived in relative poverty after housing costs in 2022-23. Despite high average incomes, many households fall below 60% of median income, particularly after paying high rents
items.markingKey: Context (Around 4 million UK children (about 30%) lived in relative poverty after housing costs in 2022-23.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline one way in which Estonia's flat income tax shows average and marginal tax rates.
items.answer: Estonia has used a flat personal income tax since 1994 (currently 22% in 2025), with a basic tax-free allowance. With a tax-free allowance, a flat marginal rate still produces an average rate that rises with income, so the system is mildly progressive

items.answer: Great Gatsby curve

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "universal basic income (UBI)"?
options: A regular, unconditional cash payment made by the government to every citizen regardless of income or employment
A curve showing the cumulative percentage of income (or wealth) received by cumulative percentages of the population, ranked from poorest to richest
Technological progress that raises the demand for, and wages of, highly skilled workers relative to low-skilled workers
A UNDP/OPHI index measuring acute poverty through deprivations in health, education and living standards (10 indicators); a person is poor if deprived in at least one-third of weighted indicators
items.answer: A regular, unconditional cash payment made by the government to every citizen regardless of income or employment
items.markingKey: A. "universal basic income (UBI)" is a regular, unconditional cash payment made by the government to every citizen regardless of income or employment.

items.stem: Which of these countries has one of the highest income Gini coefficients in the world?
items.answer: South Africa
items.markingKey: South Africa. South Africa's Gini is about 0.63 (World Bank).

items.stem: Explain the difference between absolute poverty and relative poverty.
items.answer: Absolute poverty is income below the level needed for basic needs, the same real threshold everywhere; relative poverty is income below a percentage of the national median, so it rises with the country's income level.
items.markingKey: Absolute poverty is income below the level needed for basic needs, the same real threshold everywhere; relative poverty is income below a percentage of the national median, so it rises with the country's income level. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the average tax rate and the marginal tax rate.
items.answer: The marginal rate is the tax on the last (additional) dollar of income; the average rate is total tax as a percentage of total income.
items.markingKey: The marginal rate is the tax on the last (additional) dollar of income; the average rate is total tax as a percentage of total income. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why discrimination can be a cause of poverty.
items.answer: Groups facing discrimination in labour markets, education or credit (by gender, ethnicity or caste) receive lower wages and fewer opportunities, reducing their incomes regardless of ability.

items.stem: Briefly explain why conditional cash transfers may reduce poverty in the long run as well as the short run.
items.answer: They raise current income, and the conditions (school attendance, health care) build children's human capital, raising their future earning power and breaking poverty traps.

items.answer: The Gini is a single summary number; Lorenz curves can cross, so one country may have a very poor bottom 20% and the other a very rich top 1%, yet the same area A.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how progressive taxation and transfer payments shift the Lorenz curve, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Lorenz curve for pre-tax income further from the line of equality and post-tax-and-transfer Lorenz curve closer to it; Gini falls.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline a Lorenz curve and how the Gini coefficient is derived from it.
items.answer: Cumulative % of population (x) against cumulative % of income (y); 45° line of perfect equality; Lorenz curve below it; Gini = A/(A + B), where A is the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve; a curve further from the diagonal means more inequality.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Cumulative % of population (x) against cumulative % of income (y); 45° line of perfect equality; Lorenz curve below it; Gini = A/(A + B), where A is the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve; a curve further from the diagonal means more inequality. items.stem: A student claims that a flat tax of 20% on all income is progressive because higher earners pay more dollars in tax. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Progressivity depends on the average rate rising with income; with a flat 20% the average rate is constant, so the tax is proportional (unless there is a tax-free allowance).
